title: Knowledge check: Integrating R with Other Systems

questions.prompt: For “Integrating R with Other Systems”, which approach best supports a reliable result?
options: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
Trust the first output without inspecting its inputs.
Hide warnings and skip validation to make the result look clean.
Change several unrelated parts at once so the cause of any result is unclear.
questions.answer_key: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
questions.explanation: Integrating R with Other Systems is one step in Databases, APIs, and External Integrations; external data access adds authentication, network, schema, rate-limit and cleanup requirements. Reliable work makes assumptions visible and checks behavior before scaling up.

questions.prompt: Which item is explicitly listed under “Integrating R with Other Systems” in the source curriculum?
options: Change unrelated settings before checking the input
Assume one example proves every edge case
Skip validation when the output looks plausible
questions.explanation: The source PDF lists “Calling Command-Line Programs” as part of lesson 172. The lesson retains the original topic wording.

questions.prompt: When applying “Integrating R with Other Systems” to real work, what should you do before relying on the result?
options: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
Assume missing and malformed inputs never occur.
Use the same method regardless of data type or the research question.
Remove inconvenient observations without recording the decision.
questions.answer_key: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
questions.explanation: Use approved endpoints, parameterized queries, minimal permissions, timeouts and safe handling of credentials. Record assumptions and known limitations instead of presenting a demonstration as proof.
